claims.text: A stepwise, controlled aging treatment can produce coherent nanoprecipitates in a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Producing coherent nanoprecipitates will simultaneously increase tensile strength and ductility relative to the as-cast eutectic alloy.
The as-cast baseline has a single-phase eutectic structure.
The initial alloy has a conventional dual-phase or eutectic microstructure lacking controlled nanoscale precipitates.
A tailored thermal aging treatment is the intervention used to induce coherent nanoprecipitates.
Optimal aging temperature and time should yield a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates.
The proposed strength-ductility benefit should occur at room temperature.
The intervention may also provide useful properties at moderate elevated temperatures.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength through precipitation hardening.
Coherent precipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations that could otherwise initiate premature cracks.
Stress relief and dislocation transmission at coherent interfaces help maintain or improve tensile ductility.
The treatment may increase yield and tensile strength by approximately 20–30%.
The treatment will maintain or modestly increase tensile ductility.
The synergistic benefit requires aging parameters precisely tuned to produce coherent rather than incoherent or overgrown precipitates.
Precipitate coarsening or formation of brittle phases may eliminate the simultaneous strength and ductility benefit.
The optimal aging window may be narrow because nanoprecipitation kinetics in eutectic systems are complex.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the as-cast eutectic baseline as single-phase, whereas the material_initial_state describes it as a conventional dual-phase or eutectic microstructure.
